title: Breaking News: Optum at Home May Be Shutting Down
subtitle: Sources report UnitedHealth Group's reorganization continues...
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists didn’t intend to be a real, primary news source. But thanks to TikTok, I have. My accidental beat has become UnitedHealth Group and its relentless— and somewhat clandestine —employment and corporate restructuring practices.

I first broke the story last year about Optum shutting down Optum Virtual Care, which the company denied…and then confirmed. This involved a fist bump with Endpoints News.

Well, I have another story for you, not because I want it but because—apparently—once you make one TikTok video, people approach you with information from inside the company ever onward.

A brief overview: UnitedHealth Group is the largest healthcare company on earth, known for classy moves like alleged insider trading, including the now-murdered Brian Thompson as a named party. Now, my routine disclosure:

Murder is not acceptable as a way to address disputes with a corporate entity, I remind readers.

Other UHG hit policies include massive cyber attacks that paralyzed practice cash flows and ruthlessly collecting on loans for problems caused by their carelessness, which put practices in an excellent position to be acquired for pennies on the dollar by UHG!

UnitedHealth Group owns Optum, a subsidiary that provides a dizzying array of services, including Optum at Home. Here is how United tells the story of what Optum at Home does:

“I drive a hundred or more milers per day, and I do that three to four days a week,” Linda [a nurse] said. “My office lets me see the world and I get to go meet people where they’re comfortable, in their home.”

Linda works primarily with UnitedHealthcare’s dual special needs (D-SNP) population, those that qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. This population tends to have more health challenges, including multiple chronic conditions and barriers to accessing care — making them a good candidate for in-home visits.

It sounds so very wholesome! They even bought the domain name https://www.homeandcommunity.com for these services.

My source reports…

UHG is closing HBMC and Optum at Home by end of month. We were told in a scripted meeting today. Some will be moved into other positions. The rest will get let go 4/24 I’m told. I came across your profile when looking for anyone that mentioned it.

I did mention it. The description of the meeting was classic Optum:

It was a 2 min meeting. …UHG has decided to break ties with HBMC

HBMC (home based medical care)….

Is a proactive, patient-centric, in-home care solution that improves outcomes and addresses many of healthcare’s major cost drivers.

So, of course, that had to go. The source continues:

…and Optum at Home. Legacy Optum at Home patients will remain, these are… external contracts. This will happen by end of month and they will have more details in the coming weeks. Our VP then thanked us for getting on the call and hung up. She never has done that. With every rif she stays on as long as we need to answer questions.

RIF is short for “reduction in force”…that means layoffs…the source continues:

My source for the 24th is higher up in HBMC and is reliable. Our department also had all PTO removed for that day as of yesterday afternoon. I’ve heard the redeployment will happen for some but no idea how many. … I do not want retaliation if I don’t loose my job yet.

I have confirmed this person's identity and employment to the best of my ability.

The changing healthcare landscape for UnitedHealth Group might have something to do with the fact that, at their unimaginable scale, regulatory changes in Medicare, like no longer allowing for telemedicine visits in most specialties, may have doomed this business model.

It's also possible that their Medicare Advantage business just wasn't making as much money from these at home visits as they had hoped, or it's plausible that the relentless Department of Justice investigations into them, although yielding no meaningful prosecution or enforcement actions, simply turned up the temperature too much for the company to continue what has been alleged to be criminal in several separate cases.

The DOJ has never made a nasty case against UHG—at least nothing that will move the needle on a $500bish empire. However, perhaps decisions have to be based around some degree of risk management? UHG started using the federal WARN Act database again after one newsletter author pilloried them enough, and that was the right thing to do.

The world could be a remarkably better place if the world's largest healthcare company reliably made more appropriate decisions. I hope this next round of layoffs is conducted with compassion and in keeping with the law.

Let’s keep advocating that they do so appropriately. It is also true that at the scale of UnitedHealth Group, the wind blowing on one reimbursement model or another can leave thousands out of a job and millions searching for who will take care of them now. This is a problematic system for some of the most vulnerable people.
